plannedCharts.title: India's climate line has moved
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The core answer: the national climate is warmer than the recent normal, not just in one bad summer.

plannedCharts.title: Three datasets tell the same warming story
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: This answers the cherry-picking objection: the warming signal is not a quirk of one dataset.

plannedCharts.title: India has warmed about as much as the world
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: This answers the 'India is not warming fast' claim with a fair cross-country comparison.

plannedCharts.title: Every region is warming, but not the same way
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The national average hides different regional climates and different lived risks.

plannedCharts.title: The warming map is uneven
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: People live in states, not in an all-India average, and warming has not landed evenly.

plannedCharts.title: The pre-monsoon heat window matters most
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: March-May is when heat stress peaks before rain relief arrives, so seasonal warming matters more than annual warming alone.

plannedCharts.title: 2026 so far belongs in its own box
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The current year is a live hook, but partial years must be compared only with the same months in earlier years.

plannedCharts.title: The nights are not cooling like they used to
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Warm nights are what make heat hard to recover from: the body, the house and the city never get a proper reset.

plannedCharts.title: The hottest days are a regional story
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A national annual average cannot tell a farmer in Rajasthan or a street vendor in Delhi how many punishing days they face.

plannedCharts.title: Humidity turns heat into body stress
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The danger is not only thermometer heat. Humidity decides whether sweat can cool the body.

plannedCharts.title: The monsoon has become a sharper risk
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India does not live on annual rainfall alone. It lives on whether the monsoon arrives, pauses, dumps or fails.

plannedCharts.title: Rainy days are not moving together across India
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Annual rain totals miss whether rain is spread across usable days or squeezed into fewer bursts.

plannedCharts.title: Heavy-rain days are the drainage problem
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The lived rain risk is often an overloaded drain, a flooded road or a crop field waterlogged in one spell.

plannedCharts.title: The wettest five-day spell is getting heavier
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Reservoirs, drains and fields feel clustered rain, not just seasonal totals.

plannedCharts.title: The monsoon still carries most of the year's rain
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The monsoon matters because so much of India's annual water arrives in one season.

plannedCharts.title: IMD's long monsoon record shows why averages mislead
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: ERA5 gives the gridded climate layer; IMD's observed monsoon record is the historical reality check.

plannedCharts.title: 2026 is hot and drier so far, but only through May
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The current-year section should show heat and rainfall together, while being explicit that the monsoon is not complete.

plannedCharts.title: Groundwater stress makes weak rain harder to absorb
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Climate risk is not only how much rain falls. It is also whether farms and cities have a water buffer when rain fails or arrives badly.

plannedCharts.title: The sea is rising on India's coasts
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: For coastal cities, climate change is not only a hot-day problem. Higher seas raise the floor under storm surge, drainage failure and chronic flooding.

plannedCharts.title: The monsoon still shows up in the harvest
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The rain story becomes a household story through crops. Even after irrigation and technology gains, monsoon rainfall is still visible in output.

plannedCharts.title: Rainfed crops take the climate hit first
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Climate damage is not evenly spread across the plate. Rainfed kharif crops are more exposed than irrigated or winter crops.

plannedCharts.title: Climate shocks reach the plate unevenly
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Food inflation is not one number in lived experience. A weak monsoon can leave cereals buffered while pulses, onions or vegetables do the damage.

plannedCharts.title: PM2.5 is still many times the safe-air guideline
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The live AQI snapshot needs a recent annual PM2.5 measure beside it, not a stale World Bank series ending in 2020.

plannedCharts.title: India's emissions are rising because development is energy-hungry
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The country is both exposed to warming and a growing contributor to the cause.

plannedCharts.title: Per person, India is still far below rich-country emissions
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A fair climate article has to hold scale and responsibility together.

plannedCharts.title: Where the emissions come from
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The solution set depends on the source: power, farms, industry and transport are different problems.

plannedCharts.title: The grid is changing, but coal still does the work
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India's climate path turns heavily on whether clean electricity grows faster than demand.

plannedCharts.title: Cooling demand rises faster than cooling access
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Heat becomes inequality when the escape route is an appliance most households do not have.

plannedCharts.title: The cooling map does not match the heat map
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The appliance people can afford is not always the appliance the climate needs. Evaporative coolers are common in the dry north and weak in humid heat.

plannedCharts.title: Where heat is hardest to survive
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A climate impact article needs to join hazard with the ability to cope. The dangerous zone is high heat risk, low cooling protection and poverty together.

plannedCharts.title: Heat hits work before it hits GDP tables
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Outdoor and insecure work turns climate from a weather story into an income story.

plannedCharts.title: Heat is already costing work hours
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: This moves from exposure to measured economic loss: heat already cuts labour capacity, especially in outdoor sectors.

plannedCharts.title: Heat deaths depend on how you count them
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The mortality record is part of the climate story because official heatstroke counts and modelled excess deaths answer different questions.

plannedCharts.title: A hotter century means more cooling load
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Cooling is the bridge between climate, household bills and the power grid.

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
